q: Why does Cheong+2020 Fig. 11 show V-cycle convergence continuing to improve from V4 to V6, while our smaller Cartesian problem saturates by V3-V4? Is this a genuine information-transport benefit from deeper coarsening on the paper's 640x64 spherical grid, or an artifact of the specific residual-tolerance / stopping criterion the paper uses?
basis: Our N=64 Cartesian MMS test saturates at V3 (11 V-cycles for V3, V4, V5, V6 all identical), while the paper reports monotone improvement all the way through V6 for their 640x64 problem. The grid-size argument (coarsest useful level ~2x2) predicts saturation, but the paper's plot doesn't show it.
next_steps: Rerun our solver on N=512 or N=1024 grid to have 8-9 useful levels, and see if V6 still saturates or continues improving. If the paper's monotone improvement persists to V6 even when the coarsest grid is trivial, that suggests something specific to the spherical-polar coordinate system or the BU8 lapse geometry.

q: How sensitive are Gmunu's absolute iteration counts (V6 ~ 40 iters) to the choice of prolongation operator (piecewise-constant vs bilinear vs higher-order)? The paper does not specify.
basis: Our first attempt with piecewise-constant prolongation completely failed to converge (residual stagnated at ~1e-4). Bilinear fixed it. If Gmunu uses piecewise-constant, that would be surprising given our result; if it uses bilinear, that should be documented for reproducibility.
next_steps: Contact the authors or dig into the (currently unlocated) source code to determine the exact prolongation stencil. Cross-benchmark piecewise-const vs bilinear vs biquadratic on the same nonlinear ψ^5 problem to quantify the sensitivity.

q: Does the paper's 24x-vs-2500x V1-to-V6 speedup ratio scale predictably with grid size N? Our Cartesian N=64 gives 26x; the paper's 640x64 gives ~2500x. Is the scaling roughly O(N) as multigrid theory predicts for the acceleration factor, or is there additional per-problem structure?
basis: Multigrid theory: V-cycle cost ~ O(N), smoother-only cost ~ O(N^{3/2}) for 2nd-order elliptic. Speedup ratio should therefore grow as sqrt(N). Paper's 640x64 has 40960 dof; our 64x64 has 4096; sqrt ratio is 3.16, but observed ratio is 2500/26 ~ 96. This is ~30x higher than sqrt(N) would predict.
next_steps: Sweep N ∈ {32, 64, 128, 256, 512} and log the V1 vs V6 iteration ratio. If the scaling is superlinear (i.e. approaches the paper's 2500x for N in the low thousands), that's evidence of a stronger-than-expected multigrid benefit for the ψ^5 nonlinearity. If it stays around sqrt(N), the paper's number reflects a much longer V1 baseline (they may have run V1 far past 10^5 iters and quoted the number to reach machine-precision tolerance).

q: How does the multigrid convergence rate on the CFC Hamiltonian constraint change as the star's compactness (M/R) approaches the BH-formation limit? The paper tests up to BU8 (rapidly rotating) but not near the compactness limit.
basis: The ψ^5 nonlinearity gets progressively harder as ψ deviates further from 1 (deep gravitational potential). Near BH formation, ψ diverges, and standard FAS may lose contraction. This is a real concern for using Gmunu for BH-formation studies.
next_steps: Extend Gmunu (or an analog solver) to a sequence of TOV-like configurations with increasing compactness up to just below the maximum-mass point, and record iterations to convergence vs compactness. Look for a knee where V6 needs > 100 iterations.

q: Where is Gmunu's public source code? The paper's abstract advertises 'open-source' and the author's page repeats the claim, but we could not locate a public repo. Without a canonical Zenodo DOI or GitHub URL, independent replication of the paper's application benchmarks (TOV eigenmodes, shocktube, migration) is effectively blocked.
basis: GitHub search, GitLab search, Bitbucket search, author page (kidcheong.github.io), and follow-up papers all fail to yield a repo URL. The Class. Quantum Grav. IOP publication does not mandate a repo deposit for numerical papers. This is a bottleneck for the entire community's ability to reproduce.
next_steps: Email Patrick Cheong (chi-kit.cheong@ligo.org, confirmed active LIGO address in paper header) directly. If located, deposit a mirror on Zenodo with DOI so future replicators do not repeat this search. Update this open-question entry with the outcome.
